ego.name: Vannevar Bush
ego.summary: Vannevar Bush was an American engineer, inventor, and science administrator who became a central organizer of U.S. scientific research and development during World War II. He led the Office of Scientific Research and Development (OSRD), helped initiate and administrate early work on the Manhattan Project, shaped U.S. science policy, and influenced computing and information science through his analog computer work and the memex concept.

connections.relationship_description: Mathematician who closely guided Bush on mathematical aspects of his circuit-theory textbook and wrote an appendix to Operational Circuit Analysis (1929).
shared_activities: mathematical consultation on operational calculus and circuit theory
connections.notes: Bush explicitly credited Wiener for guiding him around 'many a mathematical pitfall'.

connections.relationship_description: General Electric engineer who used Bush's differential analyzer to solve electric power transmission problems, representing notable industrial uptake of Bush's computational tools.
shared_activities: application of the differential analyzer to engineering calculations

connections.relationship_description: MIT president who appointed Bush vice president and dean of engineering in 1932; after early clashes they built a solid working relationship.
shared_activities: oversight of faculty/consulting policies and institutional strategy
connections.notes: They initially clashed over limiting faculty consulting, then cooperated closely.

connections.relationship_description: Earlier inventor whose microfilm indexing ideas were cited as a major influence on Bush’s memex concept.
shared_activities: conceptual influence on memex and information retrieval design
connections.notes: Influence is described as significant, though interaction was likely indirect (via prior work).

connections.relationship_description: Graduate student connected to Bush's MIT lab and differential analyzer work; produced landmark thesis applying Boolean algebra to switching circuits, catalyzing digital circuit design theory.
shared_activities: work around Bush's differential analyzer lab context

connections.notes: Shannon is described as one of Bush’s graduate students; Shannon also served as a research assistant operating the analyzer.

category_summaries.summary: Bush’s family circle—parents, two sisters, wife Phoebe Clara Davis, and two sons—formed a stable private backdrop to an unusually public career.
At MIT, Bush’s network spans mentors and administrators, close collaborators, and students tied to analog computation and early digital circuit theory.
Bush bridged industry and national science governance: Raytheon’s early commercialization, Carnegie leadership, NACA, and influential ideas behind the memex.
